title: Home｜CGLRD
text:
China-Gazetteer-LandReform

A county-level database on China’s land reform, constructed from provincial, municipal, county, and district gazetteers, to support research on land redistribution, class structure, economic history, and regional comparison.

title: Home｜CGLRD
text:
Database Highlights


Unified Statistical Framework
A unified system of data organization, variable definitions, and coding standards to improve the comparability of cross-regional research.


Based on Official Gazetteer Sources
Primarily based on newly compiled local gazetteers, with cross-validation using specialized gazetteers on agriculture, economy, and politics.


Coverage of the Full Land Reform Process
Includes information on class classification, landholding, land redistribution, and the confiscation and allocation of productive assets and property.


Standardized Variable Coding System
Preserves original records while providing standardized, structured, and source-labeled fields for comparison.


Spatial and Historical Comparison
Uses unified administrative division codes and supports GIS matching, regional comparison, and historical geography research.

title: Documentation and Usage Guidelines
text:
User Guide

Users should read the codebook and data cleaning documentation before using the database.
Users should distinguish between county-level statistical records and representative village-level surveys.
Users should maintain the distinction between original values, standardized values, and estimated values.

title: Documentation and Usage Guidelines
text:
Data Use Agreement

This database is primarily intended for academic research, teaching, and non-commercial purposes. Users should acknowledge the data source and cite the database according to the recommended citation format.
Without authorization from the project team, users may not publicly distribute, resell, or use the complete database files for commercial purposes.
Research outputs based on this database should clearly acknowledge the data source in academic papers, reports, or other publicly available materials.
The database is continuously updated and improved. Users are welcome to contact the project team regarding potential errors, questions, or suggestions.

title: Overview
text: Introducing the database background, objectives, current development status, and potential research applications.

title: Overview
text:
Research Background
Land reform was one of the most significant institutional transformations in twentieth-century China. It profoundly reshaped rural land institutions, social structures, agricultural production, and subsequent socialist transformation. In recent years, land reform and its long-term economic and social consequences have become important topics in economic history, political economy, and development economics.
However, existing research has largely relied on provincial-level statistics, case studies, or limited regional datasets. A nationwide county-level database with consistent definitions and standardized measures remains limited.
Chinese local gazetteers, compiled under the organization of local governments, provide systematic records of regional natural, economic, social, and historical development. In particular, they preserve extensive official records related to the implementation of land reform, class classification, land ownership, allocation of productive assets, and property redistribution.
By transforming gazetteer materials into a standardized and digitized database, this project aims to preserve valuable historical records while providing a systematic, reliable, and quantifiable data foundation for research on China’s land reform.

title: Overview
text:
Objectives
Based on nationwide local gazetteer materials, this project constructs a standardized county-level database on China’s land reform. Through unified data collection protocols, data processing procedures, and variable coding systems, information related to land reform recorded in local gazetteers is digitally organized and structured.
The database aims to provide searchable, standardized, and quantifiable historical data infrastructure for research in economic history, regional comparison, and related interdisciplinary fields.

Current focus: verification of existing data, supplementation of missing information, correction of errors, variable harmonization, and standardized database construction.

title: Overview
text:

Land reform and land redistribution studies
Institutional changes in land systems and rural property rights
Social stratification and class structure research
Agricultural economic history and rural development studies
Regional economic comparison and modern Chinese economic history
GIS-based spatial analysis, historical geography, and digital humanities research

title: FAQ
text:
Frequently Asked Questions
Frequently asked questions regarding administrative divisions, data sources, missing values, statistical coverage, access policies, and data feedback.




Why does the database use the 2002 administrative division system?＋


Administrative divisions during the land reform period (1946–1953) differ substantially from current administrative boundaries. Many county-level administrative units underwent later changes, including county-to-district reforms, prefecture-to-city transformations, and other administrative adjustments.
To provide a unified spatial identification standard and facilitate integration with modern GIS systems and other public databases, this project adopts the 2002 administrative division codes as the standard geographic coding system. Original administrative names recorded in local gazetteers are also preserved, and historical administrative units are linked to the corresponding 2002 administrative divisions.




How are multiple versions of local gazetteers for the same region handled?＋


The database prioritizes officially published gazetteers with more complete information and conducts cross-validation using multiple versions and other historical sources. When differences exist, the project evaluates the original text, contextual information, and related materials to determine the appropriate interpretation.




Why are some regions missing data?＋


Missing data may result from unavailable or unpublished local gazetteers, the absence of land reform records in available materials, or the presence of only qualitative descriptions without quantifiable statistics.




Why do some variables contain missing values?＋


Historical records differ across regions in terms of content and statistical standards. Some variables may not have been recorded or may not have corresponding information in the original sources.
Detailed information on missing value coding, definitions of empty values, and variable applicability can be found in the codebook and data cleaning documentation.




How can original data be distinguished from processed data?＋


The database preserves original information from local gazetteers whenever possible while applying standardized variable definitions for data organization.
Data that have undergone calculation, classification, conversion, or coding procedures are documented and identified in the documentation and codebook.




Why do some regions not have land reform records?＋


Some urban central areas had relatively small agricultural populations during the land reform period and did not conduct separate rural land reform programs. Therefore, relevant variables are recorded as “No.”




What is the difference between county-level statistics and representative village-level data?＋


Some local gazetteers only report survey data from representative villages or townships rather than county-wide statistics.
The database preserves indicators of statistical coverage, and users should select appropriate observations according to their research objectives.




Why is Tibet currently not included?＋


The timing, policy context, implementation process, and statistical framework of Tibet’s democratic reform differ significantly from land reform processes in most other regions of China. Therefore, the relevant data cannot be directly incorporated into the current land reform framework.




How can data issues be reported?＋


If users identify data errors, issues with gazetteer references, or have other suggestions, they may submit feedback through the project contact page.
The project team will review submitted information and document confirmed revisions in future version updates.

title: Data Sources and Methods
text: Describing the historical sources, data coverage, processing procedures, and documentation of data completeness.

title: Data Sources and Methods
text:
Historical Sources and Primary Materials
The database primarily draws on nationwide newly compiled local gazetteers, supplemented by specialized gazetteers and other publicly available historical materials. Information related to land reform is systematically extracted, organized, and standardized.
Local gazetteers are important historical documents compiled under the organization of local governments. They provide systematic records of regional economic, social, political, and historical development, and preserve extensive official information on land reform implementation, class classification, land ownership, allocation of productive assets, and property redistribution.
This database utilizes land reform-related records from agricultural, land, political, economic, and other relevant sections of local gazetteers to reconstruct county-level land reform data.
Main source types include:

County, municipal, prefectural, and provincial gazetteers
Specialized gazetteers on agriculture, land, economy, politics, and related topics
Other publicly available historical materials used for cross-validation and supplementary verification

title: Data Sources and Methods
text:
Data Coverage
The core materials consist of the first round of newly compiled local gazetteers published mainly during the 1980s and 1990s. These sources provide relatively comprehensive official records concerning the period around 1949 and the early stage of reform and opening-up, including extensive statistical information related to land reform.
The second round of newly compiled local gazetteers published after 2000 is mainly used as supplementary material.

title: Data Sources and Methods
text:
Examples of Original Gazetteer Materials
Land reform information in the database is primarily extracted from textual descriptions and statistical tables contained in local gazetteers. To demonstrate the relationship between original historical materials and database variables, this section presents examples of original gazetteer records, including land reform-related textual descriptions and statistical tables.

Land Reform Statistical Tables

Local gazetteers preserve extensive statistical information from the land reform period, including the number of households and population by social class, land area, land ownership patterns, and land redistribution outcomes.
Based on unified variable definitions, the project extracts relevant information from these materials and transforms them into standardized and structured database variables.


Textual Records on Land Reform

In addition to statistical tables, local gazetteers contain detailed textual descriptions of land reform processes, class classification, and policy implementation.
Through manual identification, coding, and standardization, these qualitative records are transformed into structured variables for quantitative analysis.

title: Data Sources and Methods
text:
Gazetteer Data Completeness
Due to differences in compilation periods, regional historical conditions, and preservation status, the completeness of land reform records varies across regions.



Category 1


Complete Records
Contains information on land reform experiences, class classification, land ownership, land redistribution, and productive assets.




Category 2


Partial Records
Contains partial textual descriptions or some quantifiable information related to land reform.




Category 3


Missing Records
Relevant information is unavailable due to absent records, missing sections, or inaccessible materials.

title: Data Sources and Methods
text:
Provincial Coverage and Administrative
The database currently covers 30 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities in mainland China. County-level administrative units are used as the basic observation units, with historical administrative adjustments incorporated into a unified coding system.
For administrative changes such as the transformation of prefectures into cities or the creation of new municipal districts, the database follows historical administrative boundaries to ensure consistency and comparability across time.
